availableTools.description: Why the tool surface looks the way it does: current airlock mode, which tools are active, and the recent history of tools appearing or disappearing with the reason for each change. Call this when a tool you expected is missing.

Write your current read of the incident into the console so the operator can see it: what you believe is happening and why. Use ruledOut for what you considered and rejected, and advisesAgainst to name an action that would be harmful — if the operator reaches for it, they see your reasoning first. Changes nothing, blocks nobody, needs no approval.

summary.description: What you believe is happening, and the evidence for it.

ruledOut.description: An action you considered and rejected, and why.

advisesAgainst.description: An action you believe would be harmful, as tool:target (e.g. deploy.rollback:d-201). If the operator reaches for it they see your reasoning first.

availableTools.description: Propose an ORDERED sequence of 2-8 actions when the order itself matters — when doing the same steps in a different order would cost more. Give the reason the order is load-bearing; the operator reads it before approving anything. Each step is still approved separately, and step N+1 is not proposed until step N has run, so nothing executes ahead of the human.

reason.description: Why THIS order. What goes wrong if the steps are taken the other way round?

steps.description: The actions in the order they must happen. 2 to 8 of them.

tool.description: The propose_* tool for this step, e.g. propose_rate_limit

because.description: What this step buys, in one line

availableTools.description: Propose taking ownership of the incident so other responders stand down. Creates an approval card; nothing happens until the operator approves.
Propose a severity for the incident. Severity decides who gets woken up and what customers are told, so it is the operator call.
Propose paging another team. This wakes a real person, so use record_finding to say why the evidence justifies it.

team.description: Team to page, such as database on-call

availableTools.description: Propose silencing alerting while the incident is worked, or turning it back on. Silence hides a genuinely new alert too.

silenced.description: true to silence, false to restore

availableTools.description: Propose text to publish on the public status page. TOP RUNG: the only action that leaves the building, and it cannot be unsaid. Write it as a customer would want to read it.

text.description: What customers are told. Plain, specific, no internal jargon.

availableTools.description: Propose a feature-flag change (tier 3 of the write ladder). Creates an approval card for the human operator; nothing changes until they approve. Check list_changes for current flag states first.
Propose freezing (or unfreezing) deploys across all services. A freeze also blocks the fix you may be about to ship.

frozen.description: true to freeze, false to lift

availableTools.description: Propose changing how much traffic a deploy serves. Raising it widens the blast radius of a bad build; lowering it narrows it without a full rollback.

deployId.description: Deploy id from list_deploys

availableTools.description: Propose capping a route. Sheds load by rejecting real customers; buys time without fixing a cause.

Propose rolling back a live deploy so its superseded predecessor becomes live again (tier 1: deploy). Requires human approval; the world rejects it if no predecessor exists. Read list_deploys — including migration metadata — before proposing.

deployId.description: Deploy id to roll back, e.g. from list_deploys

availableTools.description: Propose shipping the next build of a service (tier 1: deploy). Requires human approval. Use when the fix should move forward instead of reverting.
Propose setting an environment variable (tier 2: env). The value is stored redacted. Requires human approval.

value.description: New value (redacted in all logs and reads)

availableTools.description: Propose retargeting a route (tier 4: route/DNS — the top of the write ladder). Requires human approval AND the dual key held by the operator while it executes.
Propose moving a share of a route to another target. Check traffic_history first: moving traffic to a target with the same fault moves the outage rather than ending it.
Propose draining a route so it serves nobody. Stops the bleeding at the cost of availability for those customers.
Propose restarting a service. Drops every in-flight request and empties warm caches and pools, so expect a spike before it settles.
Propose changing replica count. New instances start cold, so capacity arrives after they warm rather than immediately.
Propose flushing a cache. Every key refills at once, which against a saturated backend is a thundering herd and makes things worse.
Propose promoting a database replica. Writes are refused during promotion and any replica lag is lost. You cannot put it back.

availableTools.description: Propose retargeting a route (tier 4: route/DNS — the top of the write ladder). Requires human approval AND the dual key held by the operator while it executes.
Propose moving a share of a route to another target. Check traffic_history first: moving traffic to a target with the same fault moves the outage rather than ending it.
Propose draining a route so it serves nobody. Stops the bleeding at the cost of availability for those customers.

Propose changing replica count. New instances start cold, so capacity arrives after they warm rather than immediately.

Propose promoting a database replica. Writes are refused during promotion and any replica lag is lost. You cannot put it back.

trajectory.text:
Here’s the ordered plan and why the order matters:

Reason for this order:
- Turning off the new-checkout flag first immediately stops the risky path from creating more v2-format session rows, narrowing the blast radius while we work.
- Then rolling the api service forward restores read compatibility with the existing v2-format rows, and can be canaried with less live pressure.
- If we reversed the order, the risky path would stay live during deploy warm-up or any hiccups, potentially widening impact and producing more incompatible data.

Steps, in order:
1) Feature flag: Turn new-checkout off.
   - Because: Quench the risky path and stop further v2-only writes from the checkout flow.
2) Deploy: Roll the api service forward.
   - Because: Ship the api build that can read the v2 sessions layout and restore compatibility.

messages.content: Plan this in order and say why the order matters: first turn the new-checkout flag off, then roll the api service forward.

args.reason: Turn the flag off first to stop the problematic path and narrow blast radius while the deploy is in flight. With new-checkout off, we stop creating more v2-layout session rows via that flow, reducing incompatibility with api 1.9.x (which reads v1 only per mig-77). Rolling the api forward second restores read-compatibility with the v2 layout and can be canaried safely with less live pressure. Reversing the order would keep the risky path active during the deploy warm-up and, if the rollforward hiccups, would prolong or widen customer impact.

steps.because: Quench the risky path and stop further v2-only writes from the checkout flow.
Ship the api build that can read the v2 sessions layout and restore compatibility.

trajectory.text:
Here’s the ordered plan and why the order matters:

Reason for this order:
- Turning off the new-checkout flag first immediately stops the risky path from creating more v2-format session rows, narrowing the blast radius while we work.
- Then rolling the api service forward restores read compatibility with the existing v2-format rows, and can be canaried with less live pressure.
- If we reversed the order, the risky path would stay live during deploy warm-up or any hiccups, potentially widening impact and producing more incompatible data.

Steps, in order:
1) Feature flag: Turn new-checkout off.
   - Because: Quench the risky path and stop further v2-only writes from the checkout flow.
2) Deploy: Roll the api service forward.
   - Because: Ship the api build that can read the v2 sessions layout and restore compatibility.

availableTools.description: Propose capping a route. Sheds load by rejecting real customers; buys time without fixing a cause.

availableTools.description: Propose shipping the next build of a service (tier 1: deploy). Requires human approval. Use when the fix should move forward instead of reverting.
Propose setting an environment variable (tier 2: env). The value is stored redacted. Requires human approval.

value.description: New value (redacted in all logs and reads)

availableTools.description: Propose retargeting a route (tier 4: route/DNS — the top of the write ladder). Requires human approval AND the dual key held by the operator while it executes.
Propose moving a share of a route to another target. Check traffic_history first: moving traffic to a target with the same fault moves the outage rather than ending it.
Propose draining a route so it serves nobody. Stops the bleeding at the cost of availability for those customers.
Propose restarting a service. Drops every in-flight request and empties warm caches and pools, so expect a spike before it settles.
Propose changing replica count. New instances start cold, so capacity arrives after they warm rather than immediately.
Propose flushing a cache. Every key refills at once, which against a saturated backend is a thundering herd and makes things worse.
Propose promoting a database replica. Writes are refused during promotion and any replica lag is lost. You cannot put it back.

trajectory.text:
I’ve proposed restarting the api service and it’s awaiting approval. 

Current status snapshot:
- api is degraded on version 2.0.0
- Traffic: 230 rps overall; /checkout errRate ~19.7%, /browse ~0.25%
- Estimated impact so far: ~214 users errored, $8.56 revenue lost
- An incident is already open

If you want, I can also:
- Record these findings in the console
- Propose a brief status update for customers
- Page the on-call, or rate-limit /checkout to reduce blast radius while we restart

Changes nothing, blocks nobody, needs no approval.

summary.description: What you believe is happening, and the evidence for it.

ruledOut.description: An action you considered and rejected, and why.

advisesAgainst.description: An action you believe would be harmful, as tool:target (e.g. deploy.rollback:d-201). If the operator reaches for it they see your reasoning first.

tool.description: The propose_* tool for this step, e.g. propose_rate_limit

input.summary: Rollback of api deploy d-201 (v2.0.0) is unsafe. The deploy applied migration mig-77: “sessions rows are written in v2 layout since this landed; api 1.9.x reads v1 layout only.” It also drops legacy_cart. Rolling back to d-200 (api 1.9.3) would leave live data in a format the predecessor cannot read, leading to session read failures and errors. The deploy metadata itself confirms irreversible data shape changes since go-live.
input.ruledOut: Rollback d-201 -> d-200. Predecessor cannot read v2 session layout and may depend on dropped legacy_cart; rollback would break running traffic.

I checked d-201. It applied migration mig-77: “sessions rows are written in v2 layout since this landed; api 1.9.x reads v1 layout only,” and it drops legacy_cart. Rolling back to d-200 would leave live data in a format the predecessor can’t read, causing session read failures.

I’ve recorded this in the console and advised against rollback of d-201.
